A: Where does it hurt? / B: My throat hurts.
The bare A/B exchange at the moment you sit down at the clinic — the classic opener and its expected reply format

nuance: 어디가 아프세요? is the doctor's or nurse's standard polite question to a patient: 어디가 'where (as subject)' + 아프다 'to hurt/be sick' + honorific -세요. The patient never says this to the doctor; the patient answers with a body-part subject — 목이 아파요, 배가 아파요. The critical grammar axis: 아프다 is a descriptive verb (adjective-verb), so the hurting place is the SUBJECT and takes the subject particle 가 — never 어디를 아프세요? (object particle 를 is wrong because nothing is being done to a target). Softer alternatives shift register: 어디가 아파? is 반말 for a parent with a child, 어디가 불편하세요? is a gentler front-desk variant that sounds more considerate. Note 아프다 covers both 'it hurts' and 'I am sick', so this one question opens virtually every clinic visit. English learners often calque 'what's wrong?' as 뭐가 틀렸어요? — 틀리다 means 'incorrect', not 'ill'; use 어디가 아프세요? or 어디가 불편하세요? instead.

structuredNuance.t: The doctor's or nurse's standard polite opening to a patient, using 어디가 'where (subject)' + 아프다 'to hurt/be sick' + honorific -세요. The patient does NOT say this to the doctor — the patient answers with a body-part subject: 목이 아파요, 배가 아파요. 아프다 covers both 'it hurts' and 'I am sick', so this single question opens almost every clinic visit.

어디가 아프세요? is clinic/존댓말 — only medical staff or caregivers ask it. 어디가 아파? is 반말 used by a parent to a child or between close friends. 어디가 불편하세요? is a gentler, slightly more formal variant heard at receptions and from nurses doing intake.

어디가 아프세요? focuses on physical pain (아프다 = hurt). 어디가 불편하세요? focuses on discomfort or general malaise (불편하다 = be uncomfortable), so it can also cover non-painful issues like dizziness or fatigue. The latter is gentler and more commonly used at receptions and front desks.
어디가 아프세요? → 어디가 제일 아프세요? (narrowing down the worst spot) → 어디가 불편하세요? (softer) → 어디 좀 보여 주세요 ('let me take a look').

Two traps: (1) wrong particle — learners say 어디를 아프세요? but 아프다 is descriptive, so the hurting place is the subject (가), not the object (를). (2) wrong phrase — 'what's wrong?' calqued as 뭐가 틀렸어요? — 틀리다 means 'incorrect (like an answer)', not 'unwell'. Use 어디가 아프세요? or 어디가 불편하세요?.

mistakes: Saying 어디를 아프세요? with the object particle 를.
아프다 is a descriptive verb, so the painful spot is the grammatical subject and takes 가/이. The correct form is 어디가 아프세요?
A patient using 어디가 아프세요? to the doctor.
This is the caregiver's question to the patient. As the patient you state the location yourself: 머리가 아파요 / 배가 아파요.
Translating 'what's wrong?' as 뭐가 틀렸어요?.
틀리다 means 'be wrong/incorrect' (as in an answer), not 'be ill'. For symptoms say 어디가 아프세요? or 어디가 불편하세요?

A: Where does it hurt? / B: I have a fever. Since yesterday.
Classic clinic A/B opener — note how the patient volunteers the duration in the same breath
어제부터 열이 나고 몸이 으슬으슬해요.
I've had a fever since yesterday and I feel chilly.
Everyday combo describing two co-occurring symptoms; 으슬으슬하다 = the shivery, goosebumpy feeling of a fever
아이가 밤새 열이 나서 해열제를 먹였어요.
My child had a fever all night so I gave them fever medicine.
Parent reporting to a doctor; 해열제 = fever reducer, 먹이다 = make someone take medicine
nuance: 열이 나요 is how you report a fever to anyone — literally 'heat arises' (열이 나다). Korean treats the fever as something that 'comes out', so the natural verb is 나다 (arise), not 있다 (exist) or 하다 (do). 열이 있어요 is also correct but sounds milder and more detached ('there is some heat'), whereas 열이 나요 is the everyday 'I am running a fever'. The particle is 이 (subject), never 열을 나요 — 나다 is intransitive and 열 is its subject. Register shifts by conjugation only: 열이 나 (반말), 열이 나요 (존댓말), 열이 납니다 (격식). The biggest English-speaker trap is calquing 'I have a fever' as 열을 가지고 있어요 — Korean bodies don't 'possess' symptoms; bodily phenomena 'arise' (나다) or 'exist' (있다). Partner words doctors ask about: 오한 (chills), 근육통 (muscle aches), 두통 (headache).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'heat comes out'. 실제 뜻: 'I have / am running a fever'. Korean treats fever as a phenomenon that 'arises' — the verb is 나다, not 있다 or 하다. The particle 이 is the subject marker because 열 (fever) is the subject of 나다.
열이 나요 to a doctor, nurse, or pharmacist (존댓말). 열이 나 to a friend or family member (반말). 열이 납니다 in a formal setting such as workplace screening. 열이 좀 있어요 downplays slightly — useful when you're unsure.

열이 나요 = 'a fever is arising/happening' — the active, everyday phrase. 열이 있어요 = 'there is (some) fever' — milder and more clinical-sounding, often used by a nurse checking your temperature. 고열이 나요 = 'I have a high fever' — a stronger version adding 고 (高).
열이 나요 → 열이 많이 나요 (bad fever) → 고열이 나요 (high fever) → 열이 좀 있어요 (mild, uncertain) → 열이 내려갔어요 (the fever broke).

'I have a fever' → 열을 가지고 있어요 — a calque of 'have' using 가지다 (to possess). No Korean says this about a symptom. Bodily states 'come out' (나다) or 'exist' (있다). Also watch the particle: 열이 나요 (subject 이), never 열을 나요.

mistakes: Saying 열을 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a fever'.
This literally translates English 'have' with 가지다 (to possess) and is unnatural for symptoms. Korean uses 열이 나요 ('a fever arises').
Using 열을 나요 with the object particle.
나다 ('to come out/arise') is intransitive, so 열 is the subject: 열이 나요, with 이, not 열을.
Saying 뜨거워요 to mean 'I have a fever'.
뜨겁다 describes a hot object you touch (hot coffee). Your body temperature being up is 열이 나요; 뜨거워요 about yourself sounds like your skin is burning hot to the touch.

usage: 존댓말; telling a doctor or pharmacist
반말; to a friend or family
Vivid extension for a severe headache; 깨지다 = shatter/split
examples: A: 어디가 아프세요? / B: 머리가 아파요. 어제 저녁부터요.
A: Where does it hurt? / B: I have a headache. Since last night.
The textbook A/B clinic exchange — note the patient adds the duration naturally
아침부터 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요.
My head's been throbbing since this morning.
Everyday use showing the mimetic adverb 지끈지끈 = the rhythmic, throbbing-ache sensation that is common with headaches
머리가 너무 아파서 회사를 조퇴했어요.
My head hurt so much I left work early.
Fuller real-life consequence; 조퇴하다 = leave work or school early due to illness
nuance: 머리가 아파요 is the everyday Korean 'I have a headache': body-part + subject particle 가 + 아파요. The subject particle 가 is mandatory because 아프다 is a descriptive verb — the head is 'the thing that is hurting', its grammatical subject, never 머리를. This frame builds all symptom sentences: 배가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 이가 아파요. Register shifts by ending only — 머리가 아파 (반말), 아파요 (존댓말), 아픕니다 (격식). One practical ambiguity: 머리 can mean 'head' (the body part) or 'hair' — in a pain context 아파요 removes all doubt. English speakers often reach for the Sino-Korean noun 두통 and produce 두통이 있어요 — that is grammatically correct and sounds more clinical (두통 = 頭痛), but in everyday speech 머리가 아파요 is far more natural; 두통 surfaces in pharmacy requests like 두통약 주세요 (give me headache medicine). Vivid intensity variants: 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요 (throbbing), 머리가 깨질 것 같아요 (splitting), 머리가 띵해요 (dull, foggy).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'my head is sick/hurting'. 실제 뜻: 'I have a headache'. The body-part + 가/이 + 아파요 frame is the universal symptom pattern — plug in any body part: 목이, 배가, 이가, 등이.
머리가 아파요 to a doctor, pharmacist, or colleague (존댓말). 머리가 아파 to friends and family (반말). 머리가 아픕니다 in a very formal context. Using 반말 to a doctor is socially inappropriate regardless of age.

머리가 아파요 = everyday speech, immediate and natural. 두통이 있어요 = Sino-Korean clinical term (두통 = 頭痛), sounds like reading a chart. Use 머리가 아파요 to a doctor verbally; 두통 appears on packaging (두통약). 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요 adds the throbbing quality.
머리가 아파요 → 머리가 많이 아파요 → 머리가 지끈지끈 아파요 (throbbing) → 머리가 깨질 것 같아요 (splitting) → 머리가 띵해요 (dull/foggy).

Two traps: (1) wrong particle — 머리를 아파요 is wrong; use subject particle 가. (2) wrong word — over-using the formal 두통이 있어요 because 'headache' is a noun in English; in spoken Korean 머리가 아파요 is far more natural.

mistakes: Saying 머리를 아파요 with 를.
아프다 is a descriptive verb, so the body part is the subject and takes 가/이: 머리가 아파요, not 머리를 아파요.
Saying 나는 머리 아파요 dropping the particle in formal speech.
Casual speech can drop 가, but to a doctor keep it: 머리가 아파요 sounds complete and clear, while bare 머리 아파 is 반말-flavored.
Using 두통해요 as a verb.
두통 is a noun; you can't verb it with 하다. Say 두통이 있어요 or, more naturally, 머리가 아파요.

Extension; 콕콕 쑤시다 = sharp, stabbing pains at a point
examples: A: 배가 아파요. / B: 설사도 하세요?
A: My stomach hurts. / B: Do you also have diarrhea?
Bare clinic A/B — note how doctors probe for 설사 (diarrhea) or 구역질 (nausea) right after this opener
어제 회를 먹고 나서 배가 계속 아파요.
My stomach has been hurting ever since I ate raw fish yesterday.
Everyday cause-and-effect; 회 = raw fish / sashimi; the doctor needs this causal information
아침부터 배가 살살 아프더니 점심 때부터 콕콕 쑤셔요.
It started as a mild ache in the morning and since lunch it's been sharp and stabbing.
Fuller progression of pain intensity showing two mimetics: 살살 아프다 (gently aching) → 콕콕 쑤시다 (stabbing)
nuance: 배가 아파요 covers stomachache, bellyache, and cramps — 배 is the whole belly/abdomen, not the stomach organ alone. The grammar is the same as all 아프다 symptoms: subject particle 가, never 배를. To pinpoint, add 윗배 (upper abdomen) or 아랫배 (lower abdomen). One important cultural note: 배가 아프다 has an idiomatic second meaning of 'to be envious' — 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 ('when a cousin buys land, your belly hurts') is a classic proverb about envy. At a clinic the medical meaning is obvious, but if a friend says 야, 배 아프다 upon hearing good news, they mean jealousy, not illness. The English-speaker error is reaching for 위가 아파요 (胃, the stomach organ) for a general bellyache — 위가 아파요 is narrower and more clinical; for ordinary abdominal pain always use 배가 아파요. Doctors may ask about 메스껍다 (nausea), 설사 (diarrhea), or 복통 (腹痛, the clinical noun) as follow-up.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'my belly is sick'. 실제 뜻: covers any stomachache, bellyache, or abdominal cramps — 배 is the whole belly, not the stomach organ. Add 윗배 (upper) or 아랫배 (lower) to narrow it. Same grammar as all 아프다 symptoms: body-part + 가 + 아파요.

배가 아파요 to a doctor (존댓말). 배가 아파 to a friend or child (반말). 배가 아픕니다 in a formal context. Important: if you say 배 아파 among friends after someone shares good news, it can be read as 'I'm jealous' (see below) — tone and context disambiguate.
배가 아파요 (general, everyday) vs 위가 아파요 (stomach organ, clinical; 위 = 胃) vs 복통이 있어요 (腹痛, medical chart language). For spoken reporting at a clinic, 배가 아파요 is always the right starting point.

배가 아프다 idiomatically means 'to be jealous/envious' — 사촌이 땅을 사면 배가 아프다 is the proverb. If a friend says 배 아프다 after hearing your good news, they are teasing about envy, not reporting illness. At a clinic the physical meaning is unambiguous.

Two traps: (1) using 위가 아파요 for a generic bellyache — 위 is the stomach organ specifically and sounds clinical; stick with 배가 아파요. (2) wrong particle 배를 아파요 — 아프다 is descriptive, 배 is the subject: 배가 아파요.

mistakes: Saying 배를 아파요 with the object particle.
아프다 is descriptive, so 배 is the subject: 배가 아파요, not 배를.
Using 위가 아파요 for a general bellyache.
위 is specifically the stomach organ and sounds clinical. For ordinary belly/abdominal pain say 배가 아파요.
Reading every 배가 아파요 as physical pain.
It can idiomatically mean 'I'm jealous'. At a clinic it's literal, but among friends 배 아파 may tease 'I'm so envious', so let context decide.

usage: 존댓말; to a doctor or coworker
반말; to a friend, particle 에 often dropped
I have come down with a cold
I feel a cold coming on
Extension for the early, mild stage before it fully hits
examples: A: 오늘 왜 못 왔어요? / B: 감기에 걸렸어요.
A: Why couldn't you come today? / B: I caught a cold.
Everyday A/B excuse — note 걸렸어요 (past) expresses the resulting present state 'I have a cold now'
애들한테 옮아서 감기에 걸렸어요.
I caught a cold from the kids.
Everyday contagion context; 옮다 = catch/be infected from someone — useful collocation
독감인 줄 알았는데 검사해 보니까 그냥 감기에 걸린 거였어요.
I thought it was the flu, but after the test it turned out to be just a cold.
Fuller situation contrasting 독감 (flu) with 감기 (cold) — a key vocabulary distinction at the clinic
nuance: 감기에 걸렸어요 means 'I caught a cold': 감기 (cold) + particle 에 + 걸리다 (to get caught/snagged) in the past tense. The particle is always 에, not 를 — you get 'caught IN' the cold like something hooking you; 감기에 걸리다 is a fixed collocation and 감기를 걸리다 is ungrammatical. Tense is a key axis: 걸렸어요 (past) conveys the resulting state 'I have a cold right now', because you got caught and are still caught. 감기에 걸려요 (present) would sound like a general tendency ('I catch colds easily') — not what you want when sick. The critical vocabulary divide: 감기 is a common cold, 독감 (毒感) is influenza — a more serious illness with a distinct test; calling the flu 감기 at a clinic seriously downplays it. For the very first hints say 감기 기운이 있어요 ('there's a hint/energy of a cold'). 옮다 ('to be infected from someone') pairs naturally: 감기를 옮았어요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'got snagged in a cold'. 실제 뜻: 'I caught / have a cold'. The metaphor is of being hooked or trapped — 걸리다 is used similarly for other ailments: 독감에 걸렸어요, 폐렴에 걸렸어요. The fixed particle is 에 (걸리다 always takes 에 for the thing you catch).

감기에 걸렸어요 to a doctor, pharmacist, or colleague (존댓말). 감기 걸렸어 to a friend or family (반말, 에 often dropped). 감기에 걸렸습니다 in a formal absence report or official context. Don't say 감기에 걸릴게요 — that would mean 'I intend to catch a cold'!

감기에 걸렸어요 (common cold, 감기) vs 독감에 걸렸어요 (flu, 독감 = 毒感). The difference is medical: 감기 is a mild respiratory illness, 독감 is influenza requiring antiviral treatment. Mixing them up to a doctor misleads them. For the onset stage: 감기 기운이 있어요 ('there is a hint of a cold coming on').
감기에 걸렸어요 → 독감에 걸렸어요 → 감기 기운이 있어요 → 감기가 다 나았어요 ('the cold is all gone') → 감기를 옮겼어요 ('I passed the cold to someone').

Two traps: (1) wrong particle — 감기를 걸렸어요 is ungrammatical; 걸리다 always takes 에. (2) wrong tense — 감기에 걸려요 sounds like a general tendency; use past 걸렸어요 when you have a cold now. (3) vocabulary confusion — never use 감기 for the flu; flu is 독감.

mistakes: Saying 감기를 걸렸어요 with 를.
걸리다 here takes 에: 감기에 걸리다 is a fixed pairing. The object particle 를 is ungrammatical.
Using present 감기에 걸려요 to mean 'I have a cold now'.
걸리다 is the moment of catching it, so the past 걸렸어요 expresses the resulting state 'I have a cold'. Present tense sounds like a general tendency.
Calling the flu 감기.
감기 is a common cold; the flu is 독감. Mixing them up downplays a serious illness to a doctor.

usage: 존댓말; reporting a symptom to a doctor or pharmacist
반말; to a friend or family
Extension stressing it's persistent; ~질 않다 = just won't (stop)
examples: A: 기침이 나요. / B: 가래도 있어요?
A: I have a cough. / B: Any phlegm too?
Classic clinic A/B — 가래 (phlegm) is the immediate follow-up question; learn these paired terms together
밤에 누우면 기침이 더 심해지고 잠을 못 자요.
The cough gets worse when I lie down at night and I can't sleep.
Everyday detail showing timing and consequence; 심해지다 = get more severe
기침이 2주째 안 멈춰서 결국 병원에 갔더니 폐렴이었어요.
I'd been coughing for two weeks without stopping, so I finally went to the doctor and it was pneumonia.
Fuller real-life consequence; 2주째 = going on two weeks, 폐렴 = pneumonia — signals when to see a doctor
nuance: 기침이 나요 reports a cough using the same 나다 ('to come out/arise') + subject particle 이 pattern as 열이 나요 and 콧물이 나요 — bodily phenomena 'arise' in Korean. You can also say 기침을 해요 ('I cough', cough + 하다), but these have a subtle difference: 기침이 나요 = 'a cough is happening to me (a symptom I have)', while 기침을 해요 = 'I am coughing (an action I'm doing)'. Both are fine at a clinic. The English-speaker traps are consistent across this file: (1) possession calque 기침을 가지고 있어요 is wrong — use 나다; (2) wrong particle — 기침을 나요 treats 나다 as transitive, but it is intransitive: always 기침이 나요. Pair-words the doctor asks next: 가래 (phlegm you cough up), 콧물 (runny nose), 호흡 곤란 (breathing difficulty). Common partner phrase from the pharmacy: 기침에 좋은 약 있어요? ('Do you have medicine good for coughs?').

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'cough comes out'. 실제 뜻: 'I have a cough / I'm coughing'. Bodily phenomena 'arise' in Korean — 기침이 나다, 콧물이 나다, 열이 나다 all share this pattern. Keep subject particle 이 (not 를): 기침이 나요.
기침이 나요 to a doctor or pharmacist (존댓말). 기침이 나 to a friend (반말). 기침이 납니다 in a formal context. It's equally natural to say to a coworker as an explanation for stepping out: 기침이 나서 잠깐 나갔다 왔어요.

기침이 나요 = 'a cough is happening (to me)' — symptom framing. 기침을 해요 = 'I am coughing' — action framing. For reporting to a doctor either works. 기침이 멈추질 않아요 adds urgency: 'it won't stop'. 마른기침이 나요 = 'I have a dry cough' (마르다 = dry).
기침이 나요 → 기침이 심해요 (the cough is bad) → 기침이 멈추질 않아요 (won't stop) → 마른기침이 나요 (dry cough) → 기침이 나아졌어요 (getting better).
Two traps: (1) 기침을 가지고 있어요 — calquing 'have a cough' with 가지다 (possess); use 기침이 나요. (2) 기침을 나요 — 나다 is intransitive, so 기침 is the subject (이), not the object (를).

mistakes: Saying 기침을 가지고 있어요 for 'I have a cough'.
This calques English 'have'. Korean says 기침이 나요 or 기침을 해요.
Saying 기침을 나요 with 를 plus 나다.
나다 is intransitive, so 기침 is the subject: 기침이 나요. (If you want 를, the verb must be 하다: 기침을 해요.)
Confusing 기침 with 가래.
기침 is the cough; 가래 is the phlegm/mucus you cough up. The doctor asks 가래도 나요? as a separate question.

usage: 존댓말; reporting a symptom to a doctor or pharmacist
반말; particle 이 often dropped with friends
Contrast extension for the opposite problem — a blocked nose
examples: A: 콧물이 나요. / B: 코도 막혔어요?
A: My nose is running. / B: Is it stuffy too?
Classic A/B — 콧물 (runny) and 코 막힘 (stuffy) are the two paired questions doctors always ask together
재채기를 계속 하면서 콧물이 줄줄 나요.
I keep sneezing and snot is running down freely.
Everyday combo; 재채기 = a sneeze; 줄줄 나다 = to run/drip continuously — the mimetic 줄줄 adds vividness
환절기만 되면 콧물이 나고 눈이 빨개지고 가렵더라고요.
Every change of season my nose runs, my eyes go red and itch.
Fuller allergy picture; 환절기 = turn-of-season period — key word for seasonal allergy context
nuance: 콧물이 나요 means 'my nose is running' — 콧물 is literally 'nose-water' (코 nose + 물 water, with the linking consonant ㅅ inserted to give 콧물), and it 'arises' using nasal particle 이 + 나다. The key contrast pair a doctor will always ask: 콧물이 나요? (runny, wet) versus 코가 막혔어요? (blocked, stuffy) — opposite problems requiring different treatments, so never confuse them. In casual speech the particle drops (콧물 나), but with medical staff say the full 콧물이 나요. The English-speaker structural trap is treating 'runny nose' as an adjective phrase and not knowing how to say it; Korean makes 콧물 (the mucus) the subject that 'comes out', so the logic is 'nose-water comes out'. Related terms to know: 재채기 (sneeze), 가래 (phlegm), 비염 (鼻炎, rhinitis — the clinical term if chronic). For allergic rhinitis a doctor may say 알레르기성 비염이에요.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'nose-water comes out'. 실제 뜻: 'I have a runny nose'. Korean makes 콧물 (the mucus itself) the subject of 나다 (to come out) — same 나다 pattern as 열이 나다, 기침이 나다. Subject particle 이, never 콧물을 나요.
콧물 = 코 (nose) + linking ㅅ + 물 (water) — a pure native Korean compound. Pronounced [콘물] due to nasalization. The clinical term is 비염 (鼻炎, 'nose inflammation') for chronic runny nose / rhinitis.
콧물이 나요 to a doctor or pharmacist (존댓말). 콧물 나 to friends and family (반말, particle dropped). 콧물이 납니다 in a formal context. To a doctor, always add how long: 콧물이 3일째 나요 ('runny for three days now').

콧물이 나요 (runny/wet nose) vs 코가 막혔어요 (blocked/stuffy nose) — opposite symptoms, different treatments. A doctor always asks both. 비염이 있어요 is the clinical self-diagnosis for chronic rhinitis. 코를 풀다 = to blow your nose (an action, not a symptom report).

English speakers try to translate 'runny nose' as an adjective phrase and get stuck. Korean treats the mucus as the subject: 콧물이 나요. Also: 콧물을 나요 is wrong (나다 is intransitive, 콧물 is the subject). And spelling: it is 콧물 not 코물 — the ㅅ is essential.

mistakes: Saying 콧물을 나요 with 를.
나다 is intransitive; 콧물 is its subject, so 콧물이 나요, never 콧물을 나요.
Confusing 콧물이 나요 with 코가 막혔어요.
콧물이 나요 = a runny (wet) nose; 코가 막혔어요 = a blocked (stuffy) nose. They are opposite symptoms.
Writing 코물 instead of 콧물.
The compound 코 + 물 inserts a ㅅ받침: it is spelled 콧물 and pronounced [콘물]. 코물 is a spelling error.

english: I feel like I'm going to throw up
usage: 존댓말; warning a doctor or nurse urgently
반말; to a friend or family
Milder extension; 메스껍다 = nauseous, queasy — less urgent
examples: A: 토할 것 같아요! / B: 잠깐, 봉투 여기 있어요.
A: I think I'm going to throw up! / B: Wait — here's a bag.
Urgent A/B exchange at a clinic or hospital ward; the urgency of 을 것 같다 is clear in the response
차만 타면 멀미가 나서 토할 것 같아요.
I get carsick the moment I'm in a car and feel like throwing up.
Everyday motion-sickness context; 멀미가 나다 = get motion sickness — a frequent cause
어지럽고 속이 울렁거려서 진짜 토할 것 같아요. 잠깐 앉아도 될까요?
I'm dizzy and my stomach is churning, I really feel like I'll throw up. May I sit down for a moment?
Fuller state with two accompanying symptoms; 울렁거리다 = stomach churning/heaving — natural co-report with 어지러워요
nuance: 토할 것 같아요 = 토하다 'to vomit' + -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 'it feels like / seems like it will happen' — the 을 것 같다 construction is crucial: it expresses an imminent, pending sensation, not a fact or a completed act. This is exactly why it's the right phrase to warn a nurse before it happens. Intensity scale: 속이 안 좋아요 (my stomach is off — mildest) → 메스꺼워요 / 울렁거려요 (queasy, churning) → 토할 것 같아요 (I'm about to throw up — most urgent). The completed act is 토했어요 (I threw up / I vomited). Casual/colloquial alternatives 게워요 or 올라올 것 같아요 are understood but avoid them with strangers — 토하다 is the neutral medical verb. The English-speaker grammar trap is loose 같아요: don't say 토해요 같아요 — 같다 must attach to the -(으)ㄹ 것 form (토할 것 같아요). Another error: using 던지다 from the English 'throw up' — 던지다 means to physically throw an object.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'it seems like I will vomit'. 실제 뜻: 'I feel like I'm about to throw up'. The -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 frame is key — it expresses an impending sensation, not a fact or completed act. Completed act: 토했어요. Impending sensation: 토할 것 같아요.

토할 것 같아요 to a doctor, nurse, or anyone nearby in a medical context (존댓말, urgent). 토할 것 같아 to friends (반말). At a clinic this phrase signals immediate action needed — nurses recognize it. The softer 메스꺼워요 is for a general 'I feel queasy' to the pharmacist.

Intensity scale: 속이 안 좋아요 (stomach's off, mildest) → 메스꺼워요 / 구역질이 나요 (nauseous, queasy) → 울렁거려요 (stomach churning) → 토할 것 같아요 (about to throw up, most urgent). Use the right level — 토할 것 같아요 triggers immediate nursing action.
토할 것 같아요 → 속이 메스꺼워요 (queasy) → 구역질이 나요 (nauseous) → 토했어요 (did throw up) → 속이 안 좋아요 (stomach's off, mildest).
Two traps: (1) 같아요 detached from 을 것 — 토해요 같아요 is wrong; 같다 must bind to -(으)ㄹ 것: 토할 것 같아요. (2) 던지다 from 'throw up' — 던지다 = to toss an object; vomiting is 토하다 with no shared meaning.

mistakes: Saying 토해요 같아요 to mean 'I feel like throwing up'.
같다 must attach to the 을 것 form: 토할 것 같아요. You can't bolt 같아요 onto a finished verb.
Using 토할 것 같아요 only after you've already vomited.
The 을 것 같다 frame is for an impending feeling. If it already happened, say 토했어요.
Saying 던지다 because a dictionary glosses 'throw up' as 'throw'.
던지다 means physically throw an object. 'Throw up' (vomit) is 토하다 — a completely different verb.

usage: 존댓말; reporting to a doctor or anyone nearby
반말; to a friend or family
Formal register; note the ㅂ-irregular in action
Vivid colloquial extension; 핑 돌다 = go light-headed in a spinning sensation
examples: A: 어지러워요. / B: 일단 여기 앉으세요.
A: I feel dizzy. / B: First, please sit down here.
Immediate A/B in a clinic — the listener's response (sit down) shows this phrase triggers action
갑자기 일어나면 어지러워요. 혈압이 낮은 것 같아요.
I get dizzy when I suddenly stand up. I think my blood pressure might be low.
Everyday trigger; 갑자기 = suddenly, 혈압이 낮다 = low blood pressure — a common cause to mention
며칠째 어지럽고 속이 메스꺼워서 일도 못 하겠어요.
I've been dizzy and nauseous for days and can't even work.
Fuller picture pairing 어지러워요 with 메스꺼워요 — these two co-occur; 며칠째 = for several days running
nuance: 어지러워요 means 'I feel dizzy/light-headed'. The base adjective-verb is 어지럽다, which is a ㅂ-irregular: the final ㅂ changes to 우/워 before vowel endings, so 어지럽다 → 어지러워요 (NOT 어지럽어요). This is one of the most commonly misspelled medical words. As a descriptive verb of state, 어지러워요 stands alone — no body-part subject is needed (unlike 머리가 아파요). The near-synonym 현기증이 나요 ('I have vertigo / dizziness', 현기증 = 眩氣症) is more clinical and noun-based (the symptom 'arises' with 나다); the divide is: everyday conversational 어지러워요 vs. chart/report 현기증이 나요. When dizzy from spinning, Koreans add 핑 돌아요 for the wheeling sensation. English speakers trip on two things: (1) the ㅂ-irregular (writing 어지럽어요), and (2) reaching for 미쳐요 ('going crazy') from 'my head is spinning' — 미치다 means losing one's mind, nothing to do with physical faintness.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: '(things are) scattered/muddled'. 실제 뜻: 'I feel dizzy / light-headed'. As a descriptive verb-adjective it stands alone — no body-part subject needed. Covers both the dizzy-from-standing sensation and general vertigo.
어지럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ → 워 before 어요/은/을. Forms: 어지럽다 (dictionary) → 어지러워요 (present) → 어지러웠어요 (past) → 어지러운 (attributive). Never 어지럽어요.

어지러워요 to a doctor or anyone nearby (존댓말). 어지러워 to a friend (반말). Say it any time you feel faint — it signals the listener to help you sit. If it's chronic, add a duration: 며칠째 어지러워요. If severe, add 쓰러질 것 같아요 ('I feel like I'll collapse').

어지러워요 (everyday spoken, immediate) vs 현기증이 나요 (clinical noun-based, 현기증 = 眩氣症, fits a chart or formal report) vs 핑 돌아요 (colloquial, spinning/whirling feeling). Use 어지러워요 to describe your state; use 현기증이 나요 if a form asks you to fill in symptoms.
Two traps: (1) regularizing the ㅂ-irregular — 어지럽어요 is wrong; the ㅂ becomes 워: 어지러워요. (2) using 미쳐요 for 'my head is spinning' — 미치다 = go crazy/insane, nothing to do with feeling faint.

mistakes: Saying 어지럽어요 by regularizing the verb.
어지럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the ㅂ becomes 워 before 어요, giving 어지러워요, not 어지럽어요.
Saying 머리가 어지러워요.
어지럽다 already describes your whole head/state, so a body-part subject is redundant. Just say 어지러워요.
Using 미쳐요 for 'my head is spinning'.
미치다 = go crazy/insane. Dizziness is 어지러워요 or 현기증이 나요; 미쳐요 has nothing to do with feeling faint.

usage: 반말; only in very close relationships, unusual in a clinic setting
Could you please give me the prescription?
More polite request; 주시겠어요 = would you be so kind as to give
Extension for lost or re-issued slips; 발급하다 = to issue a document
examples: A: 처방전 주세요. / B: 여기 있습니다.
A: The prescription, please. / B: Here you are.
The textbook A/B exchange at the clinic desk; note 여기 있습니다 is the staff's natural reply
약국에 가야 하는데 처방전 주세요.
I need to go to the pharmacy — please give me the prescription.
Everyday reason; shows the Korean split system: 병원 writes the 처방전, 약국 fills it
전에 받은 처방전을 잃어버렸는데, 다시 발급해 주실 수 있어요?
I lost the prescription I got before — could you possibly reissue it?
Fuller situation; 잃어버리다 = to lose something; 발급 = issuance — a real situation for re-visits
nuance: 처방전 주세요 asks for the prescription slip: 처방전 (處方箋, 'prescription document') + 주세요 'please give me'. Korea uses a split dispensing system: the doctor (at the 병원/의원) writes the 처방전, and you take it separately to a 약국 (pharmacy) to receive the actual medicine. So saying 처방전 주세요 is specifically addressed to the doctor or clinic staff — never the pharmacist. At the pharmacy you HAND the slip over, then say 약 지어 주세요 to have it filled. The vocabulary distinctions matter: 처방전 (the slip/document) vs 처방 (the act of prescribing) vs 약 (the medicine itself). For politeness, 좀 주시겠어요? is softer than 주세요; 주실 수 있어요? is even more indirect. English speakers often bypass this system and ask for 약 at the clinic, not realizing the receipt of a slip is the intermediate step. Saying 처방전 주세요 to the pharmacist is a common foreigner mistake — at the 약국 you hand them the slip, you don't receive it.

structuredNuance.t: Asks the clinic for the prescription document: 처방전 (the slip) + 주세요 (please give). The Korean medical system is split — the doctor writes the 처방전 at the 병원, and you take it to a separate 약국 to fill. This phrase belongs at the 병원/의원 step only.

처방전 주세요 to clinic staff (존댓말, direct but polite). 처방전 좀 주시겠어요? = softer and more polite. 처방전 다시 발급해 주세요 = for lost/re-issued slips. Never use 반말 with clinic staff regardless of how you feel — the institutional setting always calls for 존댓말.

처방전 주세요 (get the slip from the doctor's office) vs 약 지어 주세요 (ask the pharmacist to fill it) vs 약 주세요 (ask for a ready-made OTC product). Mixing these up signals you don't know how the system works: you never 'receive' a 처방전 at the pharmacy.
처방전 = 處方箋 — 處方 (dispose/prescribe + way/method) + 箋 (slip of paper/document). A Sino-Korean compound. 처방 alone means the act of prescribing; adding 전 (箋) specifies the paper document.

Two traps: (1) asking for 약 at the clinic — the 병원 gives you the 처방전, not the pills; go to the 약국 for 약. (2) saying 처방전 주세요 to the pharmacist — at the 약국 you hand them the slip, you don't ask to receive one.

mistakes: Confusing 처방전 (the slip) with 약 (the medicine).
처방전 is the paper prescription from the doctor; 약 is the medicine from the pharmacy. Ask the clinic for 처방전, the pharmacy for 약.
Asking the pharmacist 처방전 주세요.
You HAND the 처방전 to the pharmacist, you don't receive it there. At the 약국 say 약 지어 주세요 or hand over the slip.
Saying 처방 주세요 instead of 처방전.
처방 is the act of prescribing; the physical slip is 처방전. Drop the 전 and it sounds incomplete.

english: Could you fill this prescription / make up the medicine?
usage: Please make up the medicine for me
존댓말; patient to pharmacist; 좀 softens the request
반말; rare in a pharmacy, used jokingly with a close friend who is a pharmacist
Could you make up the medicine, please?
More polite request form with 주시겠어요
Please fill this exactly as prescribed
Extension handing over the slip; 처방전대로 = according to / as per the prescription
examples: A: 약 좀 지어 주세요. / B: 처방전 주시겠어요?
A: Could you fill this? / B: May I have the prescription?
The standard A/B exchange at the pharmacy counter — this is essentially scripted
감기 증상이 있는데, 처방전 없이 살 수 있는 감기약 좀 지어 주세요.
I have cold symptoms — could you make up some cold medicine I can buy without a prescription?
Everyday OTC request; 처방전 없이 = without a prescription; shows that 지어 주세요 works for OTC compounding too
아이가 먹을 거라서 가루약으로 약 좀 지어 주세요.
It's for my child, so please make it up as powder medicine.
Fuller request; 가루약 = powdered medicine (easier for children); shows that 짓다 encompasses mixing/compounding to specification
nuance: 약 좀 지어 주세요 is what you say at the pharmacy counter: 약 'medicine' + 짓다 'to make/compose' + 주세요 'please (for me)'. The verb 짓다 is a rich cultural axis — it is the same verb as 밥을 짓다 (cook rice) and 집을 짓다 (build a house), reflecting the traditional pharmacy where the 한의사 or 약사 literally measured and compounded doses for you. 짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before vowel endings — 짓다 → 지어 (NOT 짓어). So it's always 약 지어 주세요, never 약 짓어 주세요. The softener 좀 transforms a bare command into a polite request — drop it and 약 지어 주세요 starts to sound curt. The dividing line from 약 주세요 ('hand me the medicine') is that 지어 주세요 implies preparation/compounding from a prescription or for described symptoms, while 주세요 is for a ready-made product off the shelf. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'fill a prescription' with 채우다 ('fill a container') — completely wrong; 약을 짓다 is the fixed idiom.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'please compose/build the medicine for me'. 실제 뜻: 'please fill/make up the medicine'. The verb 짓다 carries the sense of assembling from components — same word as cooking rice (밥을 짓다) or building a house (집을 짓다), reflecting traditional pharmacy compounding.

짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular: the ㅅ drops before vowel endings. 짓다 → 지어 (not 짓어) → 지어 주세요 (please make up). Other forms: 지었어요 (made/filled), 지을게요 (I'll make up). The error 약 짓어 주세요 is one of the most common pharmacy mistakes.

약 좀 지어 주세요 (prepare/compound medicine to order) vs 약 주세요 (hand me a ready product, e.g. a box of aspirin) vs 약 추천해 주세요 (recommend a medicine). Use 지어 주세요 when you have a prescription or are describing symptoms and want the pharmacist to select and prepare your medications.

The verb 짓다 is pure native Korean, no 한자. Its richness comes from covering three domains: building (집을 짓다), cooking (밥을 짓다), and compounding medicine (약을 짓다) — all acts of assembling components into a purposeful whole.
Two traps: (1) calquing 'fill a prescription' as 채우다 ('fill a container') — completely wrong; use 약을 짓다. (2) ㅅ-irregular error: 약 짓어 주세요 is wrong; the ㅅ drops: 약 지어 주세요.

mistakes: Saying 짓어 주세요 instead of 지어 주세요.
짓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb: the ㅅ drops before 어, giving 지어. So it's 약 지어 주세요.
Using 채우다 to translate 'fill a prescription'.
채우다 means fill a physical container. 'Make up medicine' is 약을 짓다 — 약 지어 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and saying just 약 지어.
Without 좀 and with 반말 it sounds like a brusque order. To a pharmacist use 약 좀 지어 주세요.

english: Take it three times a day
usage: Take it three times a day
존댓말; pharmacist or doctor to patient
Take it three times a day
반말; a parent instructing a child
하루 세 번, 한 알씩 드세요
Take one tablet three times a day
Extension adding dose; 한 알씩 = one tablet each time; 알 = tablet/pill counter
examples: A: 하루 세 번 드세요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다. 언제 먹으면 돼요?
A: Take it three times a day. / B: Okay. When should I take it?
A/B at the pharmacy counter — the patient's follow-up question about timing is natural here
이 약은 하루 세 번, 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
Take this three times a day, thirty minutes after meals.
Everyday full dosing instruction combining frequency (세 번) and timing (식후 삼십 분) — learn them together
항생제는 증상이 없어져도 하루 세 번 끝까지 다 드세요.
Even if your symptoms disappear, take the antibiotics three times a day to the very end.
Fuller clinically important advice; 항생제 = antibiotics; 끝까지 = all the way through — critical compliance instruction
nuance: 하루 세 번 드세요 is the dosing instruction heard at every pharmacy: 하루 'per day' + 세 번 'three times' + 드세요, the honorific imperative of 먹다. The number system axis is critical: 번 (times/occurrences) takes NATIVE Korean numerals, not Sino-Korean — 한 번, 두 번, 세 번, 네 번, not 일 번, 이 번, 삼 번. English speakers routinely say 삼 번 by analogy with other counting, but 번 always demands native numbers. Word order is also reversed from English: Korean says 하루 세 번 (day-first), not 세 번 하루. The verb for the patient is 드세요 (honorific, to a patient/elder) or the clinical 복용하세요; the plain 먹어 is 반말 for a child. Essential dosing vocabulary to pair: 식전 (before meals), 식후 (after meals), 식간 (between meals), 취침 전 (before bed), 한 알씩 (one tablet at a time). If you don't understand the dosing, ask: 하루에 몇 번 먹어요? ('How many times a day do I take it?').

structuredNuance.t: The universal pharmacy dosing instruction: 하루 'per day' + 세 번 'three times' + 드세요 honorific imperative. The patient's honorific verb is 드세요 (or 복용하세요 in clinical writing); the caregiver's 반말 to a child is 먹어. Pair with 식전/식후 for complete instructions.
하루 세 번 드세요 = standard pharmacy/clinic 존댓말. 하루 세 번 복용하세요 = written on labels and in clinical notes. 하루 세 번 먹어 = a parent to a child (반말). Don't use 먹으세요 to an elderly patient — 드세요 is more respectful.

번 (times/occurrences) always takes NATIVE Korean numerals: 한 번 (once), 두 번 (twice), 세 번 (3×), 네 번 (4×). Sino-Korean 삼 번 is wrong here. Contrast: 분 (minutes) and other time durations take Sino-Korean (삼십 분 = 30 min) — so the number system flips depending on the counter.

하루 세 번 드세요 (frequency only) vs 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 (timing only) — these are combined in full instructions: 하루 세 번, 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. Also: 하루 한 알씩 드세요 (one tablet per day) vs 하루 세 번 드세요 (three times per day — each use).
Two traps: (1) 삼 번 for 'three times' — 번 takes native 세 번, not Sino 삼 번. (2) reversed word order — say 하루 세 번 (day then times), not 세 번 하루.

mistakes: Saying 삼 번 instead of 세 번 for 'three times'.
The counter 번 requires native Korean numerals: 한/두/세/네 번. 'Three times' is 세 번, not Sino-Korean 삼 번.
Putting it in English order: 세 번 하루.
Korean states the larger time unit first: 하루 세 번 ('a day, three times'), not 세 번 하루.
Using 먹으세요 vs 드세요 incorrectly to an elder patient.
To a patient the honorific 드세요 (or 복용하세요) is the norm; 먹어 is 반말 for a child. Plain 먹으세요 is acceptable but 드세요 is more polite.

english: Take it thirty minutes after meals
usage: 밥 먹고 삼십 분 뒤에 먹어
Eat, then take it 30 minutes later
반말; plainer everyday wording to a child or friend
Formal/clinical with 복용하다; found on written labels
Contrast extension; 식전 = before eating; often both are needed for different medicines
examples: A: 이 약은 어떻게 먹어요? / B: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
A: How do I take this medicine? / B: Take it thirty minutes after meals.
The A/B exchange that replaces reading the label; 어떻게 먹어요? = how do I take it?
속 쓰릴 수 있으니까 꼭 식후 삼십 분에 드세요.
It can irritate your stomach, so be sure to take it thirty minutes after eating.
Everyday reasoning explaining WHY the timing matters; 속 쓰리다 = have a burning/acidic stomach
이 약은 식전, 저 약은 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. 헷갈리지 마세요.
Take this one before meals and that one thirty minutes after meals. Don't mix them up.
Fuller two-medicine instruction; 헷갈리다 = get confused — a very real danger at home with multiple drugs
nuance: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 — 식후 (食後, 'after-meal') + 삼십 분 (30 minutes) + 에 (at/on) + 드세요(take) — is printed on almost every Korean prescription bag (약봉투). The number system here is the opposite of 번: time durations with minutes use SINO-Korean numbers, so '30 minutes' is 삼십 분, not native 서른 분. The particle 에 marks a specific point in time (시간점) and must not be dropped — 식후 삼십 분 드세요 without 에 sounds incomplete. Learn the full set of timing labels found on bags: 식전 (食前, before meals), 식후 (食後, after meals), 식간 (食間, between meals, rare), 취침 전 (before bed). The medical reality: 식후 drugs taken on an empty stomach can cause 속 쓰림 (gastric burning), so the distinction from 식전 is clinically important, not just vocabulary. English speakers mix number systems (세십 분 = native+Sino hybrid) and drop 에; both errors corrupt the instruction.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'at 30 minutes after-meal, take'. 실제 뜻: 'take it 30 minutes after eating'. The phrase combines a Sino-Korean compound (식후 = 食後) + Sino numeral (삼십 = 30) + time-point particle 에 + honorific imperative 드세요.
분 (minutes) takes SINO-Korean numerals: 십 분, 이십 분, 삼십 분, 사십오 분. This is the opposite of 번 (times), which takes native Korean. Never 서른 분 (native 30 + 분).

식후 삼십 분에 드세요 = pharmacist to patient (존댓말). On prescription bags and labels: 식후 30분 (abbreviated). In clinical notes: 식후 삼십 분 복용. For a child (반말): 밥 먹고 삼십 분 뒤에 먹어. Always confirm which label applies to each pill — taking a 식후 drug on an empty stomach can cause stomach damage.

식전 (食前, before meals) vs 식후 (食後, after meals) vs 식간 (食間, between meals) vs 취침 전 (before bed). These are the four standard timing labels on Korean prescription bags. 식전 and 식후 are medically opposite — many drug interactions depend on this distinction.

Two traps: (1) mixing number systems — 세십 분 (native+Sino) or 서른 분 (native minutes) are both wrong; use Sino 삼십 분. (2) dropping the time-particle 에 — 식후 삼십 분에 드세요 without 에 sounds like an incomplete instruction.

mistakes: Using native numbers for the minutes (서른 분).
Clock/duration minutes use Sino-Korean numerals: 삼십 분, not native 서른 분.
Dropping the time particle 에: 식후 삼십 분 드세요.
The point in time needs 에: 식후 삼십 분에 드세요. Without it the timing relation is unclear.
Confusing 식전 and 식후.
식전 = before meals, 식후 = after meals. They are opposites, and the wrong one can upset your stomach.

usage: 존댓말; customer to pharmacist asking about stock
반말; asking a friend who might have some in their bag
Would you happen to have painkillers?
Softer polite form; 있나요? = is there / do you have (slightly more tentative)
Extension moving from asking about availability to actually requesting them
examples: A: 진통제 있어요? / B: 네, 어떤 통증이세요?
A: Do you have painkillers? / B: Yes — what kind of pain is it?
Real pharmacy A/B — the pharmacist asks the type of pain to recommend the right product
생리통이 너무 심한데 진통제 있어요? 아까부터 계속 아파요.
My period cramps are really bad — do you have painkillers? It's been hurting for a while.
Everyday context; 생리통 = menstrual cramps — one of the most common OTC pain reasons
타이레놀 같은 진통제 있어요? 두통이 심해서요.
Do you have a painkiller like Tylenol? I have a bad headache.
Fuller request naming a reference brand; 같은 = like/such as — useful when you don't know the Korean product name
nuance: 진통제 있어요? asks a pharmacist whether they stock painkillers — 진통제 (鎭痛劑, 'pain-suppressing agent') + 있어요? ('is there? / do you have?'). 있어요? is the natural Korean way to ask about product availability in any shop; it's far more natural than the beginner calque 가지고 있어요? ('do you personally hold?'), which sounds like you're asking whether the pharmacist has it in their pocket. Painkillers like ibuprofen and acetaminophen are sold over the counter (일반의약품) without a prescription at Korean pharmacies, so this question is practically very useful. Good vocabulary to build from the same pattern: 소화제 있어요? (digestive aid?), 해열제 있어요? (fever reducer?), 파스 있어요? (pain-relief patch?). The pharmacist will typically ask 어떤 통증이세요? ('what kind of pain?') to suggest the right product — have the answer ready: 두통 (headache), 생리통 (period pain), 근육통 (muscle ache), 치통 (toothache).

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'Are there painkillers?' 실제 뜻: 'Do you have painkillers (in stock)?' In Korean, availability at a shop is expressed with 있어요? — the subject is the product itself. This pattern works for any pharmacy request: 소화제 있어요?, 해열제 있어요?, 파스 있어요?.
진통제 있어요? to a pharmacist (존댓말). 진통제 있어? to a friend (반말). 진통제 있나요? slightly softer and more tentative. The pharmacist will follow up with 어떤 통증이세요? — prepare to name the pain type: 두통, 생리통, 근육통, 치통.

진통제 = 鎭痛劑 — 鎭 (suppress/calm) + 痛 (pain) + 劑 (medicinal agent). This naming pattern applies widely: 해열제 (解熱劑, fever reducer), 소화제 (消化劑, digestive aid), 소염제 (消炎劑, anti-inflammatory). Recognizing 劑 = medical agent helps you decode any drug name.

진통제 있어요? (general painkillers, open question) vs 두통약 있어요? (headache medicine, narrower) vs 타이레놀 있어요? (brand-specific). Moving from general to specific helps the pharmacist recommend faster. 진통제 주세요 = moving from asking to requesting — use once you see they have stock.

Two traps: (1) 가지고 있어요? — sounds like 'do you personally possess one on your person'; for shop stock use 있어요?. (2) 아픔약 — there is no such word; the correct term is 진통제, or by symptom type (두통약, 생리통약).

mistakes: Asking 진통제 가지고 있어요? for shop stock.
가지고 있다 = personally possess. To ask whether a store stocks something, use 있어요?: 진통제 있어요?
Saying 아픔약 for 'painkiller'.
There is no 아픔약. The word is 진통제, or by symptom e.g. 두통약 (headache medicine).
Confusing 진통제 with 해열제.
진통제 relieves pain; 해열제 reduces fever. They overlap in some products but ask for the right one.

english: If it's really bad, go see a doctor
usage: If it gets bad, go to the doctor
존댓말; pharmacist advising a customer at the end of a visit
If it's bad, go to the doctor
반말; a friend or older family member giving concern
많이 안 좋으시면 병원에 가 보세요
If you feel worse, please try seeing a doctor
More polite; subject honorific 좋으시면 + 가 보세요 = gentler advisory
If there's no improvement, go to the doctor
Extension using a clinical-sounding alternative; 차도가 없다 = show no improvement
examples: A: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요. / B: 네, 그럴게요. 감사합니다.
A: If it's bad, go see a doctor. / B: Okay, I will. Thank you.
The standard farewell A/B at the pharmacy; 그럴게요 = I'll do that — a natural acknowledgment
이 약 드시고도 이틀 지나도록 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요.
If you're still not better after two days on this medicine, go see a doctor.
Everyday pharmacist follow-up specifying a clear time threshold: two days is the typical benchmark
열도 있고 기침도 심하면 그냥 집에 계시지 마시고 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요.
If you have a fever and a bad cough, don't just stay home — if it gets bad, go see a doctor.
Fuller advice combining warning signs; 집에 계시지 마시고 = don't just stay at home — addresses the Korean tendency to avoid the clinic
nuance: 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 is the kindly send-off a pharmacist uses: 많이 'a lot/really' + 안 좋으면 'if (it's) not good' (conditional ~으면 on 좋다) + 병원 가세요 'go to the hospital/clinic'. Two cultural axes matter. First, 병원 in Korea refers to any medical facility — from a tiny neighborhood clinic (동네의원, 의원) to a large hospital — so 병원 가세요 simply means 'go see a doctor', not 'get hospitalized' (which is 입원하다). This genuinely confuses English speakers who picture ER visits. Second, 안 좋다 ('not good') is the standard idiomatic Korean for 'feeling unwell' — it's softer and more natural than 나쁘다 ('bad') about how a person feels; 몸이 안 좋다 is a set phrase for being under the weather. To be more polite, upgrade with subject honorific: 많이 안 좋으시면 가 보세요 (가 보세요 = 'try going', gentler than the direct 가세요). For the conditional, ~으면 must attach to the verb 좋다 (안 좋으면); 만약 is optional emphasis and not a replacement.

structuredNuance.t: The pharmacist's kindly farewell advice: 많이 'really' + 안 좋으면 'if not well' + 병원 가세요 'go see a doctor'. The conditional ~으면 must attach to 좋다 (안 좋으면). This is a fixed, caring send-off, not a command.

많이 안 좋으면 병원 가세요 = pharmacist/friend to patient (존댓말). 많이 안 좋으면 병원 가 = friend to friend (반말). More polite: 많이 안 좋으시면 병원에 가 보세요 (subject honorific 좋으시면 + softer 가 보세요). Use 가 보세요 when the person hasn't decided yet; 가세요 is more direct.

안 좋으면 (if not good/well) vs 나빠지면 (if it gets worse/worsens). 안 좋다 is the idiomatic phrase for feeling unwell; 나쁘다 about a person can sound like a character judgment ('bad person'). For health, always use 몸이 안 좋다 / 안 좋으면. 차도가 없으면 ('if there is no improvement') is a more clinical variant.

병원 in Korea covers any medical facility from a neighborhood clinic (의원 / 동네 병원) to a large teaching hospital. 병원 가세요 = 'see a doctor' not 'get hospitalized'. Actual hospitalization is 입원하다. English speakers map 병원 onto 'hospital' and picture a serious ER visit — in Korea it routinely means a five-minute walk to a local clinic.
Two traps: (1) 병원 = hospital admission — wrong; 병원 = any clinic, just 'see a doctor'. (2) omitting ~으면 from the conditional: 만약 안 좋다 병원 가세요 — 만약 alone is not a conditional; the verb needs ~으면: 안 좋으면.

mistakes: Hearing 병원 가세요 as 'go get hospitalized'.
병원 covers clinics too; it simply means 'see a doctor'. For admission you'd say 입원하다.
Saying 만약 안 좋다 병원 가세요 without the conditional ending.
'If' needs the ~으면 ending on the verb: 안 좋으면. 만약 is optional emphasis, not a replacement for 으면.
Using 나쁘면 instead of 안 좋으면 about how you feel.
For health, the idiomatic 'if you feel worse' is 안 좋으면. 나쁘다 about a person can sound like 'bad-natured'; 몸이 안 좋다 is the set phrase for feeling unwell.

english: I'm aching all over / I'm run down
usage: I ache all over / I'm run down
존댓말; describing the flu-like body-ache exhaustion state to a doctor
반말; particle 이 often dropped with friends
I have body aches and exhaustion
I feel run-down, like body aches coming on
Extension for the early warning stage before full onset; 기운 = energy/signs
examples: A: 몸살이 났어요. / B: 많이 힘드시겠어요. 푹 쉬세요.
A: I ache all over. / B: That must be really hard. Get plenty of rest.
A/B showing the empathetic response 힘드시겠어요 + 푹 쉬세요 — learn these replies together
이번 주에 무리하게 일했더니 몸살이 났어요. 온몸이 쑤시고 기운이 없어요.
I pushed too hard at work this week and now I'm aching all over — my whole body throbs and I have no energy.
Everyday cause-and-effect; 무리하다 = overexert oneself; 온몸이 쑤시다 = whole body aches; 기운이 없다 = feel drained
감기는 나은 것 같은데 아직도 몸살 기운이 있어서 움직이기가 힘들어요.
The cold seems to be better but there are still signs of body aches, and it's hard to move.
Fuller picture; 몸살 기운이 있다 = the early/residual body-ache signs; 움직이기가 힘들다 = hard to move around
nuance: 몸살이 났어요 has no clean English equivalent: 몸살 describes the run-down, aching-all-over, feverish-exhaustion state from overwork or a cold — not one symptom but a cluster of body aches, fatigue, and malaise that Koreans treat as a single identifiable experience. The verb is 나다 ('arise') in past tense — 몸살이 났어요 = 'the body-ache has arisen and I have it now', parallel to 감기에 걸렸어요. Subject particle 이 (몸살이), never 몸살을 했어요. Key distinction: 몸살 (body aches + exhaustion) vs 감기 (respiratory cold) — they frequently co-occur as 감기몸살, but 몸살 by itself is specifically the muscle-aching, drained feeling, commonly triggered by 무리하다 (overexertion). Present tense 몸살이 나요 sounds like a general tendency ('I tend to get body aches'); use past 났어요 for the current state. English speakers usually describe this piecemeal ('I'm tired and my whole body hurts') — 몸살이 났어요 captures it in one natural phrase.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'body-ache arose'. 실제 뜻: 'I am aching all over / run down (from overwork or illness)'. 몸살 covers the whole cluster — muscle aches, fatigue, malaise — with no single English word. The past tense 났어요 expresses the current resulting state, like 감기에 걸렸어요.

몸살이 났어요 to a doctor or sympathetic colleague (존댓말). 몸살 났어 to a close friend (반말). 몸살이 났습니다 in a formal absence report. The typical cause to mention: 무리해서 (from overexerting), 일을 너무 많이 해서 (from working too much), 감기 때문에 (because of a cold).

몸살이 났어요 (body-ache/exhaustion cluster, often from overwork) vs 감기에 걸렸어요 (common cold, respiratory focus) vs 감기몸살이 났어요 (both combined). 온몸이 쑤셔요 ('my whole body aches') describes the sensation in more detail but lacks the exhaustion-fatigue component of 몸살.
몸살이 났어요 → 감기몸살이 났어요 (cold + body aches) → 몸살 기운이 있어요 (early signs) → 몸살이 다 나았어요 (all recovered).

Two traps: (1) no English equivalent — learners describe it piecemeal ('I'm tired and my body hurts'); 몸살이 났어요 does this in one phrase. (2) wrong verb — 몸살을 했어요 is wrong; the collocation is 몸살이 나다, and the past 났어요 expresses the present state.

mistakes: Treating 몸살 as the same as 감기.
감기 is a respiratory cold; 몸살 is the body-ache/exhaustion state. They co-occur (감기몸살) but aren't identical.
Saying 몸살을 했어요 with 를 + 하다.
The collocation is 몸살이 나다: 몸살이 났어요. It 'arises', it isn't 'done'.
Using present 몸살이 나요 for a current case.
Like 감기에 걸렸어요, the past 몸살이 났어요 expresses the present state of having it. Present tense sounds like a general tendency.

english: Do I need to get a shot?
usage: Do I have to get a shot?
존댓말; patient asking the doctor or nurse
Do I have to get a shot?
반말; a child asking a parent, or a friend
Formal register; 합니까 = formal question ending
주사 안 맞고 약만 먹으면 안 돼요?
Can't I just take pills instead of a shot?
Extension negotiating the alternative; very natural to a doctor
examples: A: 주사 맞아야 해요? / B: 아니요, 약만 드시면 될 것 같아요.
A: Do I need a shot? / B: No, I think you just need to take the medicine.
Classic reassuring A/B at the clinic — the doctor's 약만 드시면 돼요 is the most welcome answer
독감 예방 주사 맞아야 해요? 해마다 맞아야 하나요?
Should I get the flu vaccine? Do I need to get it every year?
Everyday preventive context; 예방 주사 = preventive shot / vaccination; 해마다 = every year
열이 사흘째 안 떨어지는데 주사 맞아야 해요? 솔직히 주사는 좀 무서워서요.
My fever hasn't broken for three days — do I need a shot? Honestly I'm a bit scared of needles.
Fuller, authentic patient exchange; 사흘째 = going on three days; 무섭다 = scared — the hesitation is very real
nuance: 주사 맞아야 해요? asks whether you need an injection, and the verb choice is the essential learning point: you 'get hit by' a shot — 주사를 맞다 — using 맞다 ('to be struck/get hit'). NOT 주사를 받다 (받다 = receive a handed object) and NOT 주사를 하다 (하다 = do; this is what the nurse does TO you, from the nurse's perspective). This is one of the most universal English-speaker errors in Korean medical language. The ~아야 하다 frame means 'have to/must': 맞아야 해요? = 'do I have to get (hit/struck)'? In casual speech 해요 swaps to 돼요 (맞아야 돼요?) — both are fine and natural. The Sino-Korean word 주사 (注射) covers both the injection and the needle/syringe. Two practical extensions: 예방 주사 맞다 (get vaccinated), and 수액 맞다 (get an IV drip) — 맞다 governs all of them. Pair with 약만 먹으면 돼요? when you want to avoid needles.

structuredNuance.t: 직역: 'do I have to be hit by a shot?' 실제 뜻: 'do I need to get an injection?' The surprising verb is 맞다 ('to be struck/hit') — you are the passive recipient of the needle. The ~아야 하다 frame = 'must/have to'. In casual speech 해요 → 돼요: 맞아야 돼요?

주사 맞아야 해요? to a doctor or nurse (존댓말). 주사 맞아야 돼? to a parent or friend (반말). 주사 맞아야 합니까? in a formal context. A useful follow-up to signal fear or preference: 주사 안 맞고 약만 먹으면 안 돼요? ('Can I just take pills instead?').

주사를 맞다 (get an injection — patient) vs 주사를 놓다 (give an injection — nurse/doctor) vs 주사를 맞히다 (cause someone to get a shot — e.g. parent talking about a child). This matched-pair structure (맞다/놓다/맞히다) is unique to injection vocabulary.

주사 = 注射 — 注 (pour in) + 射 (shoot/inject). A Sino-Korean medical term. 맞다 is pure native Korean meaning 'to be hit' — the pairing of a Chinese medical noun with a native verb for being struck reflects how Korean absorbed medical vocabulary.
Two traps: (1) 주사를 받다 — 받다 = receive a handed object; needles aren't handed to you, they are inserted; use 맞다. (2) 주사를 하다 — 하다 is from the nurse's perspective (administering); as the patient, say 맞다.

mistakes: Saying 주사를 받아야 해요 with 받다.
받다 = receive a handed object. An injection uses 맞다 ('be struck'): 주사 맞아야 해요?
